blocks.text: After a night of heavy drinking, the blood alcohol of a 70 kg man falls at a roughly constant rate of the order of 15 mg/dL per hour, whether his level starts high or only moderately high. Most drugs behave differently: their concentration falls faster when it is higher. The alcohol-metabolising enzyme is working at its ceiling, and that ceiling, together with the concentration of substrate at which the enzyme reaches half of it, defines the kinetics of every enzyme.

blocks.markdown:
Enzymes lower the activation energy of a reaction without altering its equilibrium. The **velocity (v)** of an enzyme reaction is the amount of product formed per unit time. At a fixed enzyme concentration, v rises as the substrate concentration [S] rises, but not indefinitely: the curve is a **rectangular hyperbola** that levels off. The model that explains this was proposed by Michaelis and Menten. The enzyme (E) binds substrate (S) reversibly to form an enzyme-substrate complex (ES), which converts to product (P) and free enzyme:

E + S in equilibrium with ES, then ES gives E + P (rate constant k2, also written kcat).

The model assumes that the enzyme is present at a much lower concentration than the substrate, that initial velocities are measured (so product build-up and the reverse reaction can be ignored), and that ES is at steady state (it forms and breaks down at equal rates).

blocks.caption: Michaelis-Menten equation. v is the initial velocity, [S] the substrate concentration, Vmax the maximum velocity and Km the Michaelis constant (same units as [S]).

blocks.title: Km and Vmax
blocks.text: Vmax is the maximum velocity, reached when all enzyme molecules are saturated with substrate; it equals kcat times the total enzyme concentration, so it is proportional to the amount of enzyme. Km is the substrate concentration at which the velocity is half of Vmax. A low Km means that the enzyme reaches half-maximal velocity at a low substrate concentration (high apparent affinity); a high Km means the opposite. Km depends on the enzyme, the substrate, pH and temperature, but not on the enzyme concentration.

blocks.markdown:
**How substrate concentration affects velocity.** The equation has three useful regions:

- When **[S] is much less than Km**, the denominator is about Km and v is approximately (Vmax/Km) x [S]: velocity is **proportional to [S]** (first-order). Most free enzyme is waiting for substrate, so adding substrate increases velocity almost in proportion.
- When **[S] equals Km**, v = Vmax/2 by definition.
- When **[S] is much greater than Km**, the denominator is about [S] and v approaches Vmax: velocity is **independent of [S]** (zero-order) because every enzyme molecule is already working. The enzyme is saturated.

Because the curve approaches Vmax only asymptotically, it is hard to read Vmax or Km directly from a hyperbola. Reaching 90 percent of Vmax needs [S] = 9 x Km.

blocks.title: Velocity at a given substrate concentration
blocks.prompt: An enzyme has Vmax 100 micromol per minute and Km 2 mM. Calculate the initial velocity when [S] is 6 mM.

steps.text: Write the equation and identify the quantities: Vmax = 100, Km = 2 mM, [S] = 6 mM.
Check that the answer is plausible: [S] is three times Km, so v should be above half of Vmax (50) but below Vmax (100). 75 is, as expected, 75 percent of Vmax.

blocks.answer: v is 75 micromol per minute, three quarters of Vmax.

blocks.markdown: **The Lineweaver-Burk plot.** Taking reciprocals of both sides of the Michaelis-Menten equation gives a straight line when 1/v is plotted against 1/[S]. The intercepts give the parameters directly: the **y-intercept is 1/Vmax**, the **x-intercept is -1/Km**, and the **slope is Km/Vmax**. This double-reciprocal plot makes Vmax and Km easy to read from experimental data by extrapolation, although it exaggerates errors at low substrate concentrations, so modern analysis often fits the hyperbola directly.

blocks.title: Reading Km and Vmax from a double-reciprocal line
blocks.prompt: A Lineweaver-Burk line passes through the points (1/[S] = 0, 1/v = 0.05) and (1/[S] = 0.5 per mM, 1/v = 0.09), where v is in micromol per minute. Find Vmax and Km.

steps.text: The point where 1/[S] = 0 is the y-intercept, so 1/Vmax = 0.05 and Vmax = 20 micromol per minute.
Km = 0.08 x Vmax = 0.08 x 20 = 1.6 mM. Check: the x-intercept is -1/Km = -0.625 per mM, on the negative side of the axis, as it must be.

blocks.answer: Vmax is 20 micromol per minute and Km is 1.6 mM.

rows: Doubling [S] roughly doubles v; the enzyme is sensitive to changes in [S]
Zero order: v nearly independent of [S]
Enzyme saturated; only more enzyme raises v
blocks.caption: Regions of the Michaelis-Menten curve.

blocks.markdown: **Clinical meaning.** Isoenzymes of one reaction can have different Km values that suit them to different jobs. Hexokinase (in most tissues) has a low Km for glucose (of the order of 0.1 mM), so it works near Vmax even at low blood glucose, whereas glucokinase (liver) has a high Km (of the order of 10 mM), so its activity rises as blood glucose rises after a meal. Drugs and alcohol can also be eliminated by enzymes that become saturated: when the drug concentration is well above the enzyme's Km, elimination is zero-order, and a small increase in dose can cause a disproportionate rise in blood concentration.

items: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]); Km is the [S] that gives v = Vmax/2.
Vmax is proportional to the total enzyme concentration (Vmax = kcat x [E]total); Km is not.
At [S] << Km the reaction is first-order; at [S] >> Km it is zero-order.
Reaching 90 percent of Vmax needs [S] equal to 9 x Km.

blocks.title: Km is not a measure of speed
blocks.text: A low Km indicates high apparent affinity for substrate, not a fast enzyme. Velocity depends on Vmax as well as Km, and Km does not change when the enzyme concentration changes, whereas Vmax does.

points: Michaelis-Menten kinetics describe a hyperbolic relation between initial velocity and substrate concentration, with parameters Vmax and Km.
Velocity is first-order in substrate when [S] is far below Km and zero-order when [S] is far above Km.
A Lineweaver-Burk plot linearises the data: y-intercept 1/Vmax, x-intercept -1/Km.
Saturable enzymes explain zero-order elimination of alcohol and some drugs, and different isoenzyme Km values tune tissue responses.

questions.stem: An enzyme has a Km of 3 mM for its substrate. At what substrate concentration will the initial velocity equal half of Vmax?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Km is defined as the substrate concentration giving half-maximal velocity.
distractorRationale.b: Half of Km does not give half Vmax; at [S] = Km/2, v is one third of Vmax.
distractorRationale.c: At 2 x Km the velocity is two thirds of Vmax.
distractorRationale.d: At 3 x Km the velocity is three quarters of Vmax.

questions.explanation: Putting [S] = Km in the Michaelis-Menten equation gives v = Vmax x Km/(2 x Km) = Vmax/2. The definition of Km is therefore the substrate concentration at half-maximal velocity.

questions.stem: A patient taking a drug eliminated by a single liver enzyme has a plasma concentration already well above the enzyme's Km. The dose is increased by 25 percent, and the plasma concentration rises far more than 25 percent. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The enzyme is saturated, so elimination is at Vmax and cannot increase to match the higher input
Raising the dose lowered the Km of the enzyme
Elimination is first-order, so velocity rises in proportion to concentration
The enzyme concentration doubled as the dose rose

questions.correctOptionText: The enzyme is saturated, so elimination is at Vmax and cannot increase to match the higher input

distractorRationale.a: Correct: at [S] much greater than Km the velocity is near Vmax and independent of [S].
distractorRationale.b: Km does not depend on drug concentration and would not fall with dose.
distractorRationale.c: First-order behaviour occurs only when [S] is well below Km.
distractorRationale.d: There is no reason for the enzyme concentration to rise in proportion to the dose.

questions.explanation: When [S] is far above Km, almost all enzyme molecules are occupied and the velocity is close to Vmax. Elimination cannot speed up with a larger dose (zero-order kinetics), so extra dose accumulates and the concentration rises disproportionately.

questions.stem: Enzyme X has a Km of 0.1 mM for its substrate and enzyme Y has a Km of 10 mM for the same substrate. Both have the same Vmax. At a substrate concentration of 0.1 mM, which statement is correct?

options.text: Enzyme X is working at half of Vmax and Y at only about 1 percent of Vmax
Both enzymes are working at half of Vmax
Enzyme Y is working faster because its Km is larger
Both enzymes are working at Vmax

questions.correctOptionText: Enzyme X is working at half of Vmax and Y at only about 1 percent of Vmax

distractorRationale.a: Correct: for X, [S] = Km so v = 50 percent Vmax; for Y, v = 0.1/(10 + 0.1) = about 1 percent of Vmax.
distractorRationale.b: Only X has [S] equal to its Km.
distractorRationale.c: A larger Km means a lower velocity at low substrate, not higher.
distractorRationale.d: Neither enzyme is saturated at this substrate concentration.

questions.explanation: Enzyme X has [S] equal to Km so v is Vmax/2. For Y, v/Vmax = 0.1/(10 + 0.1), about 0.01. Low-Km enzymes are therefore more active at low substrate concentrations.

questions.stem: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot for an enzyme, the line cuts the y-axis at 0.04 and the x-axis at -0.25. Which expressions give Vmax and Km (in matching units)?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the y-intercept is 1/Vmax and the x-intercept is -1/Km.
distractorRationale.b: These are the intercepts themselves, not their reciprocals.
distractorRationale.d: The x-intercept is -1/Km, so Km is 1/0.25, not 0.25.

questions.explanation: The y-intercept of the double-reciprocal plot equals 1/Vmax, so Vmax = 25. The x-intercept equals -1/Km, so Km = 1/0.25 = 4.

questions.stem: True or false: if the total concentration of an enzyme is doubled while substrate remains saturating, Vmax doubles but Km is unchanged.
questions.explanation: Vmax equals kcat multiplied by the total enzyme concentration, so doubling the enzyme doubles Vmax. Km is a property of the enzyme-substrate pair under given conditions and does not depend on how much enzyme is present.

questions.stem: An enzyme has Vmax of 200 micromol per minute and Km of 5 mM. Calculate the initial velocity at a substrate concentration of 15 mM.
questions.explanation: Apply v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) = 200 x 15 / (5 + 15) = 3000 / 20 = 150 micromol per minute. This is 75 percent of Vmax because [S] is three times Km.

questions.stem: A purified enzyme has a Vmax of 100 micromol per minute. When the substrate concentration is 4 mM the measured velocity is 40 micromol per minute. Calculate Km in mM.
questions.explanation: Rearrange v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) to Km = [S](Vmax/v - 1) = 4 x (100/40 - 1) = 4 x 1.5 = 6 mM. Check: with Km 6 mM, v = 100 x 4/(6 + 4) = 40, as given.

questions.stem: An enzyme in a tissue has a Km of 0.2 mM for its substrate. What substrate concentration is needed for the enzyme to operate at 90 percent of its Vmax? Give your answer in mM.
questions.explanation: Set v/Vmax = 0.9 = [S]/(Km + [S]). Then 0.9 Km + 0.9 [S] = [S], so [S] = 9 Km = 9 x 0.2 = 1.8 mM. Because the hyperbola approaches Vmax slowly, a large excess of substrate is needed to saturate the enzyme.

questions.stem: Describe how the initial velocity of an enzyme-catalysed reaction varies with substrate concentration, defining Vmax and Km, and explain why the curve levels off.
markingGuide: Hyperbolic curve described by v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S])
Vmax is the maximum velocity when all enzyme is saturated with substrate, equal to kcat times total enzyme concentration
Km is the substrate concentration giving v = Vmax/2; a measure of the apparent affinity (low Km, high affinity)
At [S] well below Km velocity is proportional to [S] (first-order); at [S] well above Km velocity is independent of [S] (zero-order)
The plateau occurs because each enzyme molecule can turn over substrate only at a limited rate and at high [S] all active sites are occupied, so extra substrate cannot raise v
questions.explanation: The hyperbolic shape reflects saturation: at low substrate many enzyme molecules are free, so velocity rises with substrate, but at high substrate all enzyme is in the ES form and velocity is limited by kcat. Km locates the midpoint of this transition.

questions.stem: A student measures initial velocity at six substrate concentrations. Explain how she can use a Lineweaver-Burk plot to find Km and Vmax, why this is easier than reading them from the hyperbolic plot, and one limitation of the method.
markingGuide: Plot 1/v against 1/[S]; the Michaelis-Menten equation in reciprocal form is linear: 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax
y-intercept is 1/Vmax, x-intercept is -1/Km, slope is Km/Vmax
Vmax and Km are found from the intercepts (taking reciprocals)
A hyperbola approaches Vmax only asymptotically, so Vmax is hard to read directly; a straight line can be extrapolated
Limitation: reciprocals exaggerate errors at low substrate concentrations (small v values), so points at low [S] distort the fit
questions.explanation: Taking reciprocals converts the hyperbola into a straight line, so the intercepts give Vmax and Km by extrapolation without needing to reach saturation. Its weakness is that small velocities at low [S] have large reciprocals, which magnify experimental error.
